overview: This 541-page State Department file traces American concern about Japanese espionage, military reconnaissance, propaganda, and technology acquisition from 1931 to 1939, with wartime follow-up in 1941 and later archival annotations. Its 345 documents range from citizen complaints, anonymous warnings, newspaper clippings, and anti-Japanese advocacy materials to diplomatic correspondence, military-intelligence reports, interdepartmental memoranda, investigative findings, and court records. Recurring subjects include photography and mapping of ports, bridges, railways, industrial plants, oil facilities, dams, and naval sites; suspected recruitment of agents and military personnel; Japanese outreach through schools, films, consulates, publications, and community organizations; the Matsuda, Miyazaki–Thompson, and Farnsworth cases; and attempts to obtain sensitive technical or biological materials. Collectively, the records reveal both genuine counterintelligence concerns and the federal government’s frequent skepticism toward sensational, weakly supported, or racially charged allegations.
interest: The file is especially valuable because it preserves the full spectrum of prewar threat perception: substantiated espionage prosecutions and suspicious efforts to obtain technical information sit beside rumors, mistaken identities, personal vendettas, and sweeping anti-Japanese claims. The internal memoranda show officials testing evidence, negotiating jurisdiction among State, War, Navy, Justice, immigration, postal, and local authorities, and balancing security against diplomatic consequences. Particularly striking are the detailed Rockefeller Institute records concerning Japanese Army surgeon Ryoichi Naito and the attempted acquisition of virulent yellow-fever virus, later reconsidered after Pearl Harbor as a possible biological-warfare warning. Historians can also use the file to study how counterintelligence became entangled with racial prejudice, debates over Japanese American loyalty, propaganda fears, and the growing expectation of conflict with Japan.
